title: Mengzi — the Chinese text
author: mencius
attributionNote: Attributed to Mencius (Meng Ke, c. 372–289 BCE) and compiled by his disciples, who frame the seven books and supply the dialogue in which he appears.
description: The Mengzi is the second of the Four Books and the fullest statement of Confucian ethics: human nature is good, and its four sprouts — compassion, shame, deference, and the sense of right and wrong — grow when they are tended. Across seven books Mencius argues with kings, farmers, rival philosophers and his own disciples about benevolent rule, the people's right to judge a tyrant, and the cultivation of the heart.
historicalContext: Written in the Warring States period, when Mencius travelled from court to court offering a moral policy no ruler adopted. Zhu Xi placed it beside the Analects, the Great Learning and the Mean in the twelfth century, and it held that place in the examination curriculum until 1905. This record is the Chinese text alone.
availabilityNote: Complete in the Chinese Text Project's transcription: 14 books, 690 paragraphs, streamed from ctext.org one book at a time. This is the original Chinese, not a translation. When the site cannot be read, the chapter is served from the library's validated import cache.
